title: Bram Underhill and the Glass Compass
body:

Bram Underhill had lived in the valley of Greybirch long enough to know which doors stuck in winter and which neighbours lied politely about it, and so when a clock that counts down to a kindness turned up, plain as a fact and impossible as a rumour, Bram Underhill understood at once that ignoring it would cost more than chasing it. The morning after the discovery, the town's ordinary business went on as usual, which was itself the strangest part: bakers baked, ferries left on time, and nobody mentioned the thing that had changed the shape of the day. Bram Underhill packed a bag, left a note that said only where the spare key was, and set out before courage could be talked out of the plan.

On the road Bram Underhill met a market inspector with a nose for forged provenance, who joined the walk for reasons of their own and stayed for reasons they would only explain later, after the second river crossing. Together they traced the trouble to a syndicate trading in stolen first drafts, whose scheme was tidy, profitable and quietly ruinous: it took something that belonged to everyone and charged everyone to use it. The confrontation was not a duel but a negotiation held in a room with no exits and too many witnesses, where Bram Underhill laid out the evidence piece by piece — a receipt, a timetable, a letter in a familiar hand — until the scheme's tidiness unravelled in public. There was a moment, sharp as a snapped string, when the outcome could have gone either way, and Bram Underhill chose the harder sentence over the easy silence.

What followed was repair rather than triumph: the taken thing was returned in instalments, apologies were made in the right order, and the town agreed on new rules written down where anyone could read them. Bram Underhill came home changed in the small ways that matter — slower to promise, quicker to notice, fond of the ordinary morning light — and put a clock that counts down to a kindness on a shelf where it could do no more harm and no more good than an honest reminder.
